papers.title: MorphoANOVA: Dissecting Histology-Gene Expression Relationships in Spatial Transcriptomics
papers.summary: MorphoANOVA is a computational method designed to link histological image features extracted from tissue sections with gene expression patterns measured in spatial transcriptomics data. It likely uses statistical approaches like ANOVA to identify which morphological features (such as cell shape, tissue structure, or staining patterns) correlate significantly with specific gene expression signatures. This allows researchers to systematically connect what tissue looks like under the microscope with the underlying molecular activity driving that appearance.
papers.why: This tool could help correlate neuronal and perineuronal net morphological features with spatial gene expression, directly supporting efforts to connect tissue histology to mitophagy/autophagy-related transcriptional signatures in brain regions of interest.

papers.title: Sleep promotes neuronal autophagy for intracellular clearance
papers.summary: This paper investigates how sleep influences autophagy, the cell's natural process for clearing damaged components, in neurons. The researchers likely found that sleep actively promotes the formation and function of autophagy machinery within brain cells, helping clear cellular debris and maintain neuronal health. This suggests sleep serves a critical housekeeping role at the cellular level, linking behavioral states to intracellular quality control mechanisms in the brain.
papers.why: This directly informs the mitophagy and autophagy in neurons component of the project by establishing a physiological trigger (sleep) that regulates these clearance pathways in vivo, which could inform experimental design around circadian timing and tissue collection for spatial transcriptomic/metabolomic analyses.

papers.title: spaDWGCN: a spatial distance weighted graph convolution network for accurate spatial tissue structure identification.
papers.summary: spaDWGCN is a deep learning method that uses a graph convolutional network weighted by spatial distance to analyze spatial transcriptomics data. It aims to improve identification of distinct tissue structures by better incorporating the spatial relationships between cells or spots. This type of model falls into the growing category of AI tools designed to extract spatial patterns from omics data more accurately than standard clustering approaches.
papers.why: This tool could help analyze spatial transcriptomics data in brain tissue to delineate structures like interneuron-rich regions or perineuronal net-associated domains with improved accuracy.

papers.title: Statistical significance testing for spatial domain detection in spatial transcriptomics
papers.summary: This paper addresses the problem of determining whether spatial domains identified in spatial transcriptomics data are statistically significant, rather than artifacts of clustering algorithms or noise. It proposes a statistical framework or test to validate spatial domain boundaries, helping researchers distinguish true biological structure from random variation in spatially resolved gene expression data. This is a methodological contribution aimed at improving the rigor of spatial domain detection pipelines commonly used in spatial transcriptomics analysis.
papers.why: Rigorous statistical validation of spatial domains is essential for confidently mapping interneuron subtypes and perineuronal net-associated niches in spatial transcriptomics data, ensuring that downstream biological interpretations are not based on spurious clustering artifacts.

papers.title: Hippocampal CA1 TOM70 Overexpression Attenuates Type 2 Diabetes-Associated Cognitive Impairment and Enhances Mitochondrial Quality Control in Mice
papers.summary: This study looks at how boosting a protein called TOM70 in the hippocampal CA1 brain region affects cognitive problems caused by type 2 diabetes in mice. TOM70 is involved in bringing proteins into mitochondria and helping cells manage mitochondrial health. The researchers found that increasing TOM70 levels improved memory and learning deficits in diabetic mice, likely by enhancing mitochondrial quality control processes like mitophagy.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it directly examines mitophagy and mitochondrial quality control in neurons within a disease-relevant hippocampal context, aligning with the core mitophagy/autophagy focus of the PhD project even though it lacks spatial omics or interneuron/PNN components.
papers.figure: A figure showing mitophagy markers (e.g., PINK1/Parkin or LC3-mitochondria colocalization) in CA1 neurons with and without TOM70 overexpression under diabetic conditions.

papers.title: AMPK/PINK1/Parkin pathway-associated mitochondrial quality control contributes to magnesium sulfate-induced neuroprotection in postoperative cognitive dysfunction.
papers.summary: This study investigates how magnesium sulfate protects the brain against postoperative cognitive dysfunction (POCD), a condition sometimes seen after surgery and anesthesia. The researchers found that magnesium sulfate activates the AMPK/PINK1/Parkin signaling pathway, which helps cells identify and remove damaged mitochondria through a process called mitophagy. By improving this mitochondrial quality control system, magnesium sulfate appears to reduce neuronal damage and cognitive decline in animal models of POCD.
papers.why: This paper provides direct mechanistic insight into PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy in neurons, a core pathway relevant to the mitophagy focus of the PhD project, even though it lacks spatial omics or interneuron/PNN components.
papers.figure: A figure showing immunostaining or quantification of mitophagy markers (e.g., PINK1, Parkin, LC3) in neurons across treatment groups would be most informative.

papers.title: Pharmaco-genetic evidence of presymptomatic lysosomal dysfunction coupled to detrimental DPR secretion in Drosophila Models of C9orf72-linked ALS/FTD.
papers.summary: This study uses Drosophila models of C9orf72-linked ALS/FTD to investigate how dipeptide repeat proteins (DPRs) produced from the mutant gene affect cellular health. The researchers find evidence that lysosomal dysfunction occurs early, before symptoms appear, and is linked to harmful secretion of DPRs between cells. They combine genetic and pharmacological approaches to probe these mechanisms, suggesting lysosomal/autophagic pathways as potential therapeutic targets.
papers.why: This paper's focus on lysosomal and autophagic dysfunction as an early, presymptomatic driver of neurodegeneration is directly relevant to the mitophagy/autophagy mechanisms being studied in neurons, even though it uses a fly ALS/FTD model rather than spatial omics in brain tissue.

papers.title: Integrated single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomics define tumour cell metaprograms and tumour microenvironment organisation in choroid plexus tumours.
papers.summary: This paper uses single-nucleus RNA sequencing combined with spatial transcriptomics to study choroid plexus tumours, a rare type of brain tumour. The researchers identify distinct tumour cell metaprograms, which are recurring patterns of gene expression that define different tumour cell states. They also map how these tumour cells are organised in space relative to surrounding microenvironment components like immune cells and stroma.
papers.why: This paper is tangential to the profile since it focuses on tumour biology rather than neuronal mitophagy or interneurons, but the spatial transcriptomics methodology applied to brain tissue could offer useful technical approaches for the PhD project.
